planting.note: Plant tubers shallowly, flat side down, in gritty, well-drained, humus-rich soil in dry shade under deciduous trees; wonder cyclamen flowers in September and October just before the leaves emerge.

directions: Plant dormant tubers just beneath the soil surface in late summer in sharply drained, humus-rich soil under deciduous trees, where they receive a dry, shaded summer rest and a cool, moist autumn-to-spring growing season. Cyclamen mirabile is readily told apart from the more common Cyclamen hederifolium by its rounded leaves, which have a coarsely toothed or scalloped margin and often emerge flushed with rose-pink and bronze before settling into their mature silver-and-green marbling. The pale to deep pink, twisted-petaled flowers appear singly on short stems in early autumn, usually just ahead of the first leaves, and self-sown seedlings slowly form a naturalized colony once established. Keep the planting site dry through summer dormancy, since rot is the chief hazard of overwatering while the tuber is resting.

planting.note: Plant tubers in a sheltered, sharply drained shady spot with deep leaf litter; false ibericum cyclamen flowers earliest of the spring-blooming hardy species, often starting in late winter.

directions: Plant tubers in a sheltered site with deep, humus-rich, sharply drained soil under a canopy of shrubs or deciduous trees, replicating the deep leaf litter of its native Turkish forests. Cyclamen pseudibericum produces the largest and most richly colored flowers of the winter-into-spring hardy cyclamen, a deep carmine-magenta with a darker basal stain and a narrow white rim around the mouth, carried above heart-shaped, toothed, silver-patterned leaves from late winter into mid-spring. It is somewhat less reliably hardy than C. coum and resents combined winter wet and cold, so a raised, well-drained site or the shelter of a wall improves survival outdoors in zone 7. Where winters are consistently wet and freezing, grow it in a pot in a cold frame or unheated greenhouse instead.

planting.note: Plant tubers shallowly in very well-drained, gritty soil in bright shade; Libyan cyclamen is the most cold-tender of the commonly grown hardy cyclamen species and needs protection below zone 9.

directions: Plant tubers just beneath the surface of very sharply drained, gritty soil in bright, open shade, giving the plant a distinctly dry summer rest followed by cooler, moister autumn growth. Cyclamen rohlfsianum is immediately recognizable by its broad, maple-like leaves — wider than long, deeply lobed, and toothed, in plain green or patterned with silver — which appear alongside or slightly after the fragrant, deep-pink, dark-nosed autumn flowers that carry a distinctive protruding cone of stamens. Native to a narrow coastal range in Cyrenaica, Libya, it is the tenderest of the hardy garden cyclamen and needs winter protection or container culture anywhere colder than zone 9. Where marginal, grow it in an unheated greenhouse or cold frame and move it outdoors only for its autumn display.

planting.note: Plant tubers in a sheltered, well-drained shady spot on a slope or raised bed; Lebanon cyclamen tolerates hard frost but not the combination of winter cold and standing wet.

directions: Plant tubers on a sheltered slope or raised, humus-rich, sharply drained site in shade, since Lebanon cyclamen comes from steep, rocky, north-facing limestone ravines where drainage is fast even though rainfall is fairly heavy. Dull grey-green, heart-shaped leaves with faint silvery marbling emerge in autumn and persist through winter, and pale pink to white flowers with a deeper pink mouth open in late winter into early spring before fading with the onset of summer dormancy. It has proven hardier than once assumed, tolerating short spells well below freezing in a sheltered spot, but wet, poorly drained soil in cold weather is quickly fatal. Where winters are cold and wet rather than merely cold, grow it in a pot under glass instead of in the open garden.
